screens.title: Integrating Azure Data Services and Advanced Scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to join Azure data services into a coherent, secure, and governed data platform. We focus on practical integration patterns: using Azure Data Factory to orchestrate ETL and ELT across storage, databases, Synapse, and Databricks; securing service access with Private Link and Managed Identities to remove credentials from code; scaling relational workloads using cross-database and elastic queries; and cataloging and governing data with Azure Purview. You will also see how to reason about real-time needs where Azure Stream Analytics fits. Each pattern has trade-offs: orchestration gives repeatability, Private Link reduces internet exposure but adds DNS and network complexity, and Purview adds lineage visibility at the cost of initial classification work. A concrete example you will return to is building a pipeline that copies CSV sales data from Data Lake Storage Gen2 into an Azure S Q L Database table while authenticating without secrets. Throughout, I’ll flag common mistakes such as underestimating network configuration and skipping robust error handling. By the end you’ll be able to choose which service to use, how to connect them securely, and how these choices affect operations and compliance. What integration will you plan first in your environment?

Integrating Azure Data Services

Create reliable pipelines, protect access to PaaS services, and govern data so teams can trust what's being produced. We'll use cards and step patterns to show how pieces fit together into production solutions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your work on integration, security, scaling, and governance. First, you will learn how to integrate Azure Data Factory for ETL and ELT pipelines across on-premises and Azure services, so you can automate ingest, transform, and load operations reliably. Second, you'll explore advanced security patterns such as Azure Private Link and Managed Identities so your services communicate without exposing credentials or traversing the public internet. Third, you'll implement cross-database and elastic queries to scale relational data access patterns and support sharded or multi-database architectures. Finally, you will use Azure Purview to discover, classify, and trace data lineage so you can meet compliance and data-quality needs. Each objective ties to hands-on tasks: creating linked services and datasets in ADF, configuring private endpoints, enabling managed identity authentication, and registering data assets in Purview. As you practice, look for the operational impacts of these choices: network configuration and monitoring must be planned up front. Which objective will you tackle first in your lab?

screens.title: Azure Data Factory Pipelines: Activities and Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Data Factory is the orchestration fabric for batch and scheduled movement and transformation of data. At its core a pipeline groups activities: a Copy Data activity moves data between a source and sink; a Data Flow activity applies code-free transformations running on Spark for mapping, filtering, and schema changes; and a Stored Procedure activity executes T-S Q L logic in a database when you need server-side transformation. A typical pattern is to ingest raw CSV files into a data lake, run a Data Flow to clean and convert to Parquet, then use another Copy activity to load curated data into a Synapse or Azure S Q L table. A concrete example: a Copy activity reads a sales CSV from Data Lake Storage Gen2 and writes into an Azure S Q L table; staging through Blob Storage may be enabled to handle format or size constraints. Common mistakes include not setting appropriate retry policies, neglecting schema drift handling in datasets, and running heavy transformations in Copy instead of a Data Flow or Databricks job. When planning pipelines, think about monitoring and idempotency: you want pipelines to be repeatable without duplicating data. As you author pipelines, ask: how will failures be detected and retried, and where should transformations run for performance?

keyIdea.title: ADF pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Copy for movement, Data Flow for Spark-based transformations, and Stored Procedure for server-side logic; design for retries and idempotent runs.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › ADF Activities
Process
Pipeline step sequence
1
Ingest (Copy Data)
Move raw files from source systems into Data Lake Storage Gen2.
2
Transform (Data Flow)
Run mapping data flows for filtering, type conversions and writing Parquet.
3
Load (Copy / Stored Proc)
Copy curated data into Azure SQL, or call a stored procedure to merge rows.
Example
Copy sales_data.csv → Sales staging Parquet → Load into dbo.SalesData
Common mistake
Running heavy joins in Copy activity instead of a Spark Data Flow causes performance and scale issues.
Activity JSON (conceptual)
{
  "name": "CopyDataToSynapse",
  "type": "Copy",
  "inputs": [{ "referenceName": "SourceDataset", "type": "DatasetReference" }],
  "outputs": [{ "referenceName": "SinkDataset", "type": "DatasetReference" }],
  "typeProperties": {
    "source": { "type": "AzureSqlSource" },
    "sink": { "type": "AzureSqlSink" },
    "enableStaging": true,
    "stagingSettings": { "linkedServiceName": "AzureBlobStorageLinkedService" }
  }
}
Key Takeaway
Choose the right activity for the right workload and include retries, logging, and idempotency checks in every pipeline.

screens.title: Authoring Linked Services and Datasets
screens.narratorSegment: Before you can copy data, you must create linked services and datasets that describe where data lives and how to connect. A linked service is the connection information for a service—Data Lake Storage Gen2 or Azure S Q L Database—and can use Managed Identity authentication instead of storing account keys or passwords. A dataset points to a specific file or table and contains format details like CSV delimiter or Parquet schema. For example, create an Azure Data Lake linked service that uses the factory-managed managed identity to read the sales CSV. Then create a dataset referencing the file path rawdata/sales/sales_data. csv with first row as header. For the sink, create a dataset that points to the target table [dbo].[SalesData] in your Azure S Q L Database. A useful verification step is to test the linked service connection from ADF Studio and preview a dataset sample before saving. Mistakes to avoid include leaving credentials in pipeline parameters and not importing the schema, which makes mapping fragile. After datasets are validated, drag a Copy activity into a pipeline, select source and sink datasets, click Debug to run, and inspect the output. This hands-on flow makes your integration repeatable and auditable.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Linked Services & Datasets
Definition
Linked Service

A linked service stores connection and authentication details. Prefer Managed Identity where supported to avoid embedding credentials in configs.

Definition
Dataset

A dataset represents a specific table or file and its format. Import schemas to simplify mapping and reduce runtime errors.

Example
SalesCsvDataset → AzureDataLakeStorageLS (Managed Identity)
Pro Tip
Use dataset previews and linked service test connections before running debug jobs.
Starter SQL
Run this in your Azure SQL Database to create the target table used by the sink dataset.
-- Connect to your Azure SQL Database and run this
CREATE TABLE [dbo].[SalesData] (
  OrderID INT,
  CustomerID INT,
  OrderDate DATE,
  Amount DECIMAL(10, 2)
);
Key Takeaway
Prepare the sink schema first, test linked services, and prefer managed identities to avoid secret sprawl.

screens.title: Advanced Security: Private Link and Managed Identities
screens.narratorSegment: Security for integrated services must be designed before deployment. Azure Private Link enables private endpoints for PaaS services like Azure S Q L, Azure Storage, and Synapse, bringing the service into your virtual network with a private IP. This removes exposure to public endpoints and significantly reduces attack surface. Managed Identities provide a service principal for Azure resources such as Data Factory, so the service can obtain Azure AD tokens to authenticate to other services without storing credentials in configuration. A practical example: grant the Data Factory managed identity the db_datawriter role on an Azure S Q L Database and configure the linked service to authenticate using 'Managed Identity'. This allows your Copy activity to connect securely. A common misconception is believing Private Link alone is sufficient; in practice you must also set up DNS and routing so the private endpoint resolves correctly, and you should verify Network Security Groups and firewall rules. Also, Managed Identities require role assignments and proper permissions; forgetting to grant the right database role will produce authentication errors. In planning, combine Private Link with identity-based authentication to minimize both network exposure and secret management risks, and test end-to-end connectivity before production runs.

keyIdea.text: Combine private networking with identity-based auth to remove public access and secrets from pipelines, then validate DNS and permissions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Private Link & Identities
Definition
Azure Private Link

Creates a private endpoint in your VNet so PaaS services are reached by private IP addresses and avoid public internet exposure.

Managed Identities

An Azure AD identity managed by the platform that services use to authenticate to other Azure resources without secrets.

Example
Assign Data Factory's managed identity the db_datawriter role on the target Azure SQL Database and configure the linked service to use Managed Identity authentication.
Pitfall
Neglecting DNS updates for Private Link causes services to still resolve public endpoints, breaking private connectivity.
Verification checklist
  • Confirm private endpoint has a private IP in the VNet and appropriate NSG rules.
  • Validate DNS resolution maps the service FQDN to the private IP.
  • Grant the managed identity explicit database roles and test authentication.
  • Add pipeline retries and monitoring for authentication failures.
Key Takeaway
Private Link plus Managed Identity removes both public exposure and secret management, but requires DNS and permissions checks to function reliably.

screens.title: Cross-Database Queries vs Elastic Queries
screens.narratorSegment: When relational data grows, there are two Azure patterns that let you query across multiple databases. Cross-database queries are available on Azure S Q L Managed Instance and allow a single query to span multiple databases on the same instance. This is useful when you need tight integration between databases and you control the instance boundary. Elastic queries, on the other hand, are part of Azure S Q L Database's elastic database tools and enable queries across multiple sharded databases. Elastic queries are designed for horizontally scaled, sharded applications where each shard is a separate database and you need an aggregate view or fan-out queries. A concrete example: a customer lookup service may use elastic queries to combine tenant shards for analytics, while an application with instance-scoped objects might use cross-database queries on a Managed Instance for transactional consistency. A common misconception is treating them as interchangeable: cross-database queries are not available on single Azure S Q L databases, and elastic queries introduce coordination and potential performance trade-offs for large fan-out queries. When choosing, consider administrative boundaries, required feature compatibility, and the expected query patterns. Which pattern matches your tenancy and scaling needs?

keyIdea.text: Use cross-database queries for tight instance-scoped integration on Managed Instance; use elastic queries for sharded Azure SQL Database scaling.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Cross-DB vs Elastic
Cross-Database Queries
Azure SQL Managed Instance
  • Single query spans multiple databases on the same instance.
  • Good for instance-scoped features and tight transactional integration.
  • Requires Managed Instance deployment and instance-level permissions.
Elastic Queries
Azure SQL Database (elastic tools)
  • Query across many sharded databases to aggregate results.
  • Designed for horizontal scale with separate database shards per tenant.
  • Consider query fan-out cost and coordination overhead.
Decision checklist
Match pattern to administrative boundary, feature needs, and query shape. If you need instance-scoped features use Managed Instance; if you need horizontal shard scaling use elastic queries and plan for fan-out costs.

screens.title: Azure Purview: Data Governance and Lineage
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Purview provides a single place to discover, classify, and understand where data lives and how it flows. It scans registered data sources, builds a catalog of assets, classifies sensitive data based on rules, and captures lineage so you can trace a data element from source through transformation to consumption. For a DBA, Purview answers questions like: which pipelines wrote this table, who has access to it, and where did the rows come from? A concrete scenario is onboarding your Data Factory pipelines and the target Azure S Q L tables into Purview, then running a classification scan that flags personally identifiable fields. This helps audits and downstream consumers trust the data. A common mistake is treating governance as an afterthought; skipping early classification and lineage wiring makes audits harder later. Start small: register your most critical sources, run scans, and use Purview's lineage to validate pipeline mappings. Over time the catalog becomes a source of truth for compliance, impact analysis, and data discovery across teams. What asset will you register first in Purview? Azure Purview: Data Governance and Lineage means purview gives discovery, classification, and lineage so you can trust datasets and demonstrate compliance across pipelines and databases.. In practical terms, discover, classify, and trace data across your estate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Azure Purview
What it does
Catalog, classify, and trace lineage
  • Discover assets across on-premises and cloud sources by registering data stores.
  • Classify sensitive data using built-in or custom scanning rules to support compliance.
  • Capture lineage so you can follow data from source through ADF pipelines into analytical stores.
Example
Register your Data Lake and Azure SQL, scan for PII, and use lineage to validate which pipeline produced a curated table.
Common mistake
Delaying Purview onboarding until late in a project leads to missing lineage and costly rework. Start with critical data sources first.
Key Takeaway
Treat governance as part of the pipeline: register sources, run scans, and capture lineage early to support audits and trust.

screens.title: Orchestrating Heavy Transformations with Databricks or Synapse
screens.narratorSegment: When your transformation needs exceed code-free mapping flows, you orchestrate external compute like Databricks notebooks or Synapse Spark pools from Azure Data Factory. Think of ADF as the conductor: it schedules, passes parameters, and moves data before and after heavy jobs. A common pattern is to land raw files into a data lake, trigger a Databricks job that runs Spark-based transformations, and then write curated parquet files back to the lake or load results into Synapse S Q L Pool. For example, you might use ADF to launch a Databricks notebook that joins multiple large tables, writes partitioned parquet, and then calls a stored procedure in an Azure S Q L Database to update downstream metadata. A frequent misconception is treating Databricks like a simple function: remember that cluster sizing, job concurrency, and data partitioning affect cost and performance. Another pitfall is passing secrets in parameters; use Managed Identities so ADF and compute jobs authenticate without embedded credentials. The visual shows an orchestrator node, compute nodes, and storage sandboxes with clear data movement arrows. As you design orchestration, ask: which steps require distributed compute, what is the right data partitioning strategy, and how will you validate outputs after the job completes?

keyIdea.title: Orchestrate external compute
keyIdea.text: Use ADF as the scheduler and parameter-passer while heavy transformations run on Databricks or Synapse Spark pools.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Orchestrating Heavy Transformations
Architecture
ADF as conductor, compute as worker

ADF schedules jobs, passes runtime parameters, and stages data. Databricks and Synapse Spark execute distributed transformations at scale.

Common Pattern
  • Ingest raw files to Data Lake Gen2.
  • Trigger Spark job (Databricks / Synapse) for heavy joins and aggregations.
  • Write partitioned parquet and update metadata with a stored procedure.
Pro tip: use parameterized jobs and cluster pools for cost control.
Common Mistake

Treating distributed compute as interchangeable: choose the compute type that matches your library and latency needs, and size clusters intentionally.

Architecture Diagram
Orchestration flow
Process + compute + storage
Azure Data Factory (orchestrator)

Schedules jobs, provides activities, passes parameters, and links to compute and storage.

Databricks / Synapse Spark

Execute distributed transformations. Tune cluster size and partitions for performance.

Data Lake Storage Gen2

Landing zone and partitioned output. Use parquet and partition keys that match your query patterns.

Downstream sinks

Synapse SQL Pool, Azure SQL DB, or analytics stores that consume curated data.

Takeaway
Orchestrate heavy jobs with ADF, but design compute sizing, partitioning, and authentication before production runs.

screens.title: Staging, Partitioning, and Performance Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Data movement costs both time and money if you don't design staging and partitioning carefully. When moving large tables from Azure S Q L Database into a data lake, staging to blob storage before a Spark job can reduce hot reads on the source and enable parallel ingestion. Use partitioned parquet files aligned to common query predicates so downstream analytics read only relevant partitions. In Azure Data Factory, the Copy Data activity supports enableStaging and stagingSettings to write intermediate data to blob storage, improving throughput for large transfers. Also think about parallel copy and degree of copy parallelism: too low and you waste time; too high and you overload the source or network. A misconception is that more parallel threads always reduce elapsed time; in practice, the database and network become bottlenecks. Monitor throughput, IOPS, and C P U on the source database; tune batch sizes and partition key selection accordingly. The included example JSON shows conceptual staging settings used by many teams as a reliable pattern. Finally, always test with production-like volumes and measure end-to-end latency so your pipeline meets SLA expectations.

narration.text: Data movement costs both time and money if you don't design staging and partitioning carefully. When moving large tables from Azure S Q L Database into a data lake, staging to blob storage before a Spark job can reduce hot reads on the source and enable parallel ingestion. Use partitioned parquet files aligned to common query predicates so downstream analytics read only relevant partitions. In Azure Data Factory, the Copy Data activity supports enableStaging and stagingSettings to write intermediate data to blob storage, improving throughput for large transfers. Also think about parallel copy and degree of copy parallelism: too low and you waste time; too high and you overload the source or network. A misconception is that more parallel threads always reduce elapsed time; in practice, the database and network become bottlenecks. Monitor throughput, IOPS, and C P U on the source database; tune batch sizes and partition key selection accordingly. The included example JSON shows conceptual staging settings used by many teams as a reliable pattern. Finally, always test with production-like volumes and measure end-to-end latency so your pipeline meets SLA expectations.

content.html:

When to stage

Stage when direct reads stress the source, when transformations require distributed compute, or when you need to enable parallel downstream processing.

Partitioning rules
  • Pick partition keys used by common filters (date, tenant, region).
  • Keep partition sizes balanced to avoid skew.
  • Use parquet with columnar compression for analytics workloads.
Misconception

More parallel threads always help — not true. Monitor source limits and tune concurrency to the weakest component.

screens.title: Error Handling, Retries, and Monitoring for ADF Pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: Robust pipelines anticipate failure. Azure Data Factory provides retry policies, failure paths, and diagnostic logs you should design into every pipeline. Start by adding predictable retry counts and exponential backoff to activities that call remote systems. For long-running jobs, design idempotent steps so safe replays don't duplicate data. Use a failure branch that captures error details into a shadow table or blob and triggers an alerting workflow. Observability requires telemetry: enable diagnostic settings for ADF to stream pipeline runs and activity logs into Azure Monitor Logs. From there, build queries that flag failed runs, long-running activities, high retry rates, or repeat throttling from a source database. A frequent mistake is relying solely on debug runs; production failures expose different edge cases. Another misconception is trusting email alone for notifications; pair alerts with a runbook that contains remediation steps and runbook links. In practice, test your alerts by simulating small failures, and document the playbook so on-call responders have immediate steps. Closing question: when a pipeline fails after partial writes, how will you prevent duplicate records on replay? content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Error Handling & Monitoring
Failure patterns
  1. Add retries with exponential backoff for transient errors.
  2. Make activities idempotent or add dedupe logic on ingest.
  3. Capture error payloads to a quarantine store for inspection.
Monitoring essentials
  • Stream ADF diagnostic logs to Azure Monitor Logs.
  • Create alerts for failed pipeline runs, repeated retries, or activity slowdowns.
  • Build dashboards that show throughput, latency, and error categories.
Check your understanding

If a sink table shows partial write, would you rerun the whole pipeline or replay only idempotent steps? Document your playbook for both cases.

Alert example

Alert when pipeline failure rate exceeds 1% over a sliding hour window, or when any pipeline run has more than three retries.

Runbook snippet
  • Check the failed activity logs.
  • Inspect quarantine blobs for bad rows.
  • Decide replay scope: idempotent step only or full pipeline.
Why it matters

Good observability reduces mean time to repair and prevents silent data quality issues downstream.

screens.title: Azure Stream Analytics for Low-Latency Processing
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Stream Analytics is a fully managed service for analyzing streaming data with low latency. It accepts inputs like Event Hubs and IoT Hub, runs S Q L-like streaming queries to filter, aggregate, and detect patterns, and writes results to sinks such as Azure S Q L Database, Power BI, or Data Lake Storage. Consider a telemetry scenario where devices emit sensor readings every few seconds: Stream Analytics can compute rolling averages or spot spikes and forward alerts to a database and a dashboard in near real-time. The service uses a familiar declarative style, so teams can express tumbling windows, sliding windows, and pattern matching without writing distributed code. A common misconception is to treat stream processing as a direct replacement for batch ETL; instead, use it for time-sensitive insights while keeping batch pipelines for heavy historical processing. Also account for exactly-once vs at-least-once semantics depending on your sink and windowing strategy. Practical example: detect temperature anomalies using a one-minute tumbling window and write flagged events to a S Q L table for immediate alerting. Ask yourself: what latency requirement do you truly need, and does that justify the complexity of a streaming pipeline?

Key capabilities

  • Windowing functions: tumbling, sliding, hopping.

Detect device anomalies: compute a one-minute average via a tumbling window and write records that exceed thresholds to a SQL table for alerting and investigation.

screens.title: Secure, Governed Integration Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: A production-grade platform blends secure connectivity, identity, and governance. Use Private Link to keep PaaS endpoints like Azure S Q L Database and Synapse inside your VNet and avoid public exposure. Pair that with Managed Identities so ADF, Databricks, and Functions authenticate to data stores without secrets in code. For governance, register your data stores and pipelines with Azure Purview so data discoverability, classification, and lineage are available to DBAs and data consumers. A common integration pattern is: ADF copies raw data into a Private Link–secured storage account using a managed identity; a Databricks job reads that storage using the same managed identity; Purview scans the storage, indexes schemas, and shows lineage from source systems through ADF activities into curated sinks. Beware of network complexity: Private Link can require DNS configuration and peering; teams often underestimate that setup time. Also, plan Purview classification scopes to avoid over-scanning. Practical question: when you trace lineage for compliance, how will you show which pipeline run produced a specific table partition? Answering that requires consistent metadata updates from pipelines into a catalog that Purview can index.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Secure, Governed Integration
Pattern overview

ADF orchestrates ingestion using Managed Identities to authenticate. Private Link encloses PaaS endpoints in your VNet. Purview indexes and provides lineage for compliance and discovery.

Practical steps
  1. Enable Managed Identity for ADF and grant least-privilege roles on targets.
  2. Create Private Endpoints for databases and storage and validate DNS resolution.
  3. Register sources and pipelines in Purview for classification and lineage capture.
Gotcha

Private Link requires DNS updates and may affect connectivity; plan a validation window and test service-to-service authentication early.

Example flow
ADF (managed identity) → Private Endpoint to Storage (staging) → Databricks job reads staging via MI → Purview scans staging and records lineage → Final sink is Private Link–secured Azure SQL.
Takeaway

Combine network isolation, identity-based auth, and governance to create auditable, secure data platforms that scale safely.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three concepts capture the chapter's practical guidance. First, orchestration: Azure Data Factory is the control plane that sequences data movement and triggers heavy compute. Think of ADF as the reliable scheduler that coordinates linked services, datasets, and compute activities. Second, secure connectivity: Private Link and Managed Identities work together to keep PaaS services inside your virtual network and remove credentials from code by enabling Azure AD authentication. This reduces exposure to the public internet and simplifies secret management. Third, governance and observability: Azure Purview and diagnostic streaming give you cataloging, classification, and lineage so you can prove where data came from and who touched it, while structured monitoring and alerting let you catch and fix pipeline failures quickly. Keep these three ideas in mind when designing production systems: orchestrate, secure, and govern. How will you show provenance for a critical dataset in your next pipeline?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to join Azure data services into a coherent, secure, and governed data platform. We focus on practical integration patterns: using Azure Data Factory to orchestrate ETL and ELT across storage, databases, Synapse, and Databricks; securing service access with Private Link and Managed Identities to remove credentials from code; scaling relational workloads using cross-database and elastic queries; and cataloging and governing data with Azure Purview. You will also see how to reason about real-time needs where Azure Stream Analytics fits. Each pattern has trade-offs: orchestration gives repeatability, Private Link reduces internet exposure but adds DNS and network complexity, and Purview adds lineage visibility at the cost of initial classification work. A concrete example you will return to is building a pipeline that copies CSV sales data from Data Lake Storage Gen2 into an Azure S Q L Database table while authenticating without secrets. Throughout, I’ll flag common mistakes such as underestimating network configuration and skipping robust error handling. By the end you’ll be able to choose which service to use, how to connect them securely, and how these choices affect operations and compliance. What integration will you plan first in your environment?

These objectives focus your work on integration, security, scaling, and governance. First, you will learn how to integrate Azure Data Factory for ETL and ELT pipelines across on-premises and Azure services, so you can automate ingest, transform, and load operations reliably. Second, you'll explore advanced security patterns such as Azure Private Link and Managed Identities so your services communicate without exposing credentials or traversing the public internet. Third, you'll implement cross-database and elastic queries to scale relational data access patterns and support sharded or multi-database architectures. Finally, you will use Azure Purview to discover, classify, and trace data lineage so you can meet compliance and data-quality needs. Each objective ties to hands-on tasks: creating linked services and datasets in ADF, configuring private endpoints, enabling managed identity authentication, and registering data assets in Purview. As you practice, look for the operational impacts of these choices: network configuration and monitoring must be planned up front. Which objective will you tackle first in your lab?

This second objectives slide highlights operational skills and the pitfalls teams often miss. You should learn to create linked services and datasets in ADF and test pipelines using debug runs and publish actions so that deployments are repeatable. You should also practice configuring Managed Identity authentication and Private Link endpoints, then verifying connectivity and DNS resolution, because network mistakes are the most common source of production outages. Additionally, you will practice mapping cross-database and elastic query scenarios to application needs so you can make a justified architecture choice. Finally, include Purview onboarding with classification rules and lineage ingestion to ensure audits and discovery succeed. Each skill ties directly to a hands-on checkpoint: create a Copy Data pipeline, authenticate with managed identity, configure a private endpoint, run a query across shards, and register assets in Purview. Practice these steps and you will reduce surprise outages and improve compliance posture.

Azure Data Factory is the orchestration fabric for batch and scheduled movement and transformation of data. At its core a pipeline groups activities: a Copy Data activity moves data between a source and sink; a Data Flow activity applies code-free transformations running on Spark for mapping, filtering, and schema changes; and a Stored Procedure activity executes T-S Q L logic in a database when you need server-side transformation. A typical pattern is to ingest raw CSV files into a data lake, run a Data Flow to clean and convert to Parquet, then use another Copy activity to load curated data into a Synapse or Azure S Q L table. A concrete example: a Copy activity reads a sales CSV from Data Lake Storage Gen2 and writes into an Azure S Q L table; staging through Blob Storage may be enabled to handle format or size constraints. Common mistakes include not setting appropriate retry policies, neglecting schema drift handling in datasets, and running heavy transformations in Copy instead of a Data Flow or Databricks job. When planning pipelines, think about monitoring and idempotency: you want pipelines to be repeatable without duplicating data. As you author pipelines, ask: how will failures be detected and retried, and where should transformations run for performance?

Before you can copy data, you must create linked services and datasets that describe where data lives and how to connect. A linked service is the connection information for a service—Data Lake Storage Gen2 or Azure S Q L Database—and can use Managed Identity authentication instead of storing account keys or passwords. A dataset points to a specific file or table and contains format details like CSV delimiter or Parquet schema. For example, create an Azure Data Lake linked service that uses the factory-managed managed identity to read the sales CSV. Then create a dataset referencing the file path rawdata/sales/sales_data. csv with first row as header. For the sink, create a dataset that points to the target table [dbo].[SalesData] in your Azure S Q L Database. A useful verification step is to test the linked service connection from ADF Studio and preview a dataset sample before saving. Mistakes to avoid include leaving credentials in pipeline parameters and not importing the schema, which makes mapping fragile. After datasets are validated, drag a Copy activity into a pipeline, select source and sink datasets, click Debug to run, and inspect the output. This hands-on flow makes your integration repeatable and auditable.

Security for integrated services must be designed before deployment. Azure Private Link enables private endpoints for PaaS services like Azure S Q L, Azure Storage, and Synapse, bringing the service into your virtual network with a private IP. This removes exposure to public endpoints and significantly reduces attack surface. Managed Identities provide a service principal for Azure resources such as Data Factory, so the service can obtain Azure AD tokens to authenticate to other services without storing credentials in configuration. A practical example: grant the Data Factory managed identity the db_datawriter role on an Azure S Q L Database and configure the linked service to authenticate using 'Managed Identity'. This allows your Copy activity to connect securely. A common misconception is believing Private Link alone is sufficient; in practice you must also set up DNS and routing so the private endpoint resolves correctly, and you should verify Network Security Groups and firewall rules. Also, Managed Identities require role assignments and proper permissions; forgetting to grant the right database role will produce authentication errors. In planning, combine Private Link with identity-based authentication to minimize both network exposure and secret management risks, and test end-to-end connectivity before production runs.

When relational data grows, there are two Azure patterns that let you query across multiple databases. Cross-database queries are available on Azure S Q L Managed Instance and allow a single query to span multiple databases on the same instance. This is useful when you need tight integration between databases and you control the instance boundary. Elastic queries, on the other hand, are part of Azure S Q L Database's elastic database tools and enable queries across multiple sharded databases. Elastic queries are designed for horizontally scaled, sharded applications where each shard is a separate database and you need an aggregate view or fan-out queries. A concrete example: a customer lookup service may use elastic queries to combine tenant shards for analytics, while an application with instance-scoped objects might use cross-database queries on a Managed Instance for transactional consistency. A common misconception is treating them as interchangeable: cross-database queries are not available on single Azure S Q L databases, and elastic queries introduce coordination and potential performance trade-offs for large fan-out queries. When choosing, consider administrative boundaries, required feature compatibility, and the expected query patterns. Which pattern matches your tenancy and scaling needs?

It scans registered data sources, builds a catalog of assets, classifies sensitive data based on rules, and captures lineage so you can trace a data element from source through transformation to consumption. This helps audits and downstream consumers trust the data. A common mistake is treating governance as an afterthought; skipping early classification and lineage wiring makes audits harder later. Start small: register your most critical sources, run scans, and use Purview's lineage to validate pipeline mappings. Over time the catalog becomes a source of truth for compliance, impact analysis, and data discovery across teams. What asset will you register first in Purview? A common integration pattern is: ADF copies raw data into a Private Link–secured storage account using a managed identity; a Databricks job reads that storage using the same managed identity; Purview scans the storage, indexes schemas, and shows lineage from source systems through ADF activities into curated sinks. Beware of network complexity: Private Link can require DNS configuration and peering; teams often underestimate that setup time. Also, plan Purview classification scopes to avoid over-scanning. Practical question: when you trace lineage for compliance, how will you show which pipeline run produced a specific table partition? Answering that requires consistent metadata updates from pipelines into a catalog that Purview can index.

These three concepts capture the chapter's practical guidance. First, orchestration: Azure Data Factory is the control plane that sequences data movement and triggers heavy compute. Think of ADF as the reliable scheduler that coordinates linked services, datasets, and compute activities. Second, secure connectivity: Private Link and Managed Identities work together to keep PaaS services inside your virtual network and remove credentials from code by enabling Azure AD authentication. This reduces exposure to the public internet and simplifies secret management. Third, governance and observability: Azure Purview and diagnostic streaming give you cataloging, classification, and lineage so you can prove where data came from and who touched it, while structured monitoring and alerting let you catch and fix pipeline failures quickly. Keep these three ideas in mind when designing production systems: orchestrate, secure, and govern. How will you show provenance for a critical dataset in your next pipeline?

A short checklist to use when you design or operate data platforms. First, staging and partitioning: stage large transfers and choose partition keys that align with query patterns to reduce downstream reads. Second, observability and error handling: implement retries, idempotency, quarantine handling, and stream diagnostics into Azure Monitor so you can alert and run playbooks quickly. Third, real-time needs: use Azure Stream Analytics for low-latency pattern detection and dashboards, but keep batch pipelines for historical reprocessing and large-scale aggregations. These concise reminders help you choose the right tool and design the pipeline correctly: stage for scale, instrument for reliability, and pick streaming only when latency matters.
